reference.title: will / won’t
rows: I / you / he / she / it / we / they ’ll (will) + infinitive
I’m seeing Jessica at six. – She’ll be late.
I / you / he / she / it / we / they won’t (will not) + infinitive
The film’s in French. We won’t understand anything.
Will it rain tomorrow? – Yes, it will. / No, it won’t.

reference.title: Predictions
reference.text: Use will / won’t + infinitive to make predictions, i.e. to say what you think will happen: It’s a great book. I’m sure you’ll like it. We often use I think / I don’t think / I’m sure + will: I don’t think it’ll rain tomorrow.

reference.why: With think, make the verb think negative, not will.

reference.title: be going to for predictions
reference.text: You can also use be going to for predictions, especially when you can see or know that something is going to happen: Look at the clouds. It’s going to rain. They’re playing very well. They’re going to win.

reference.title: Think positive
reference.text: A radio programme about positive thinking: callers give their tips – live in the present, think positive thoughts, don’t follow the news too much, make a list of good things every week, use positive language.

reference.title: Why negative thinking can be positive
reference.text: ‘Defensive pessimism’ (Julie K. Norem, Wellesley College) is a strategy to manage anxiety, fear, and worry: defensive pessimists imagine all the things that can go wrong in a future situation and then plan how to avoid each problem. So they are prepared and in control.

reference.title: wrong
reference.text: go to the wrong place, the wrong number; go wrong (= not happen as planned): Sometimes everything goes wrong. There’s something wrong with the printer (= it doesn’t work well).

tasks.instruction: Read the article. What is defensive pessimism? How do defensive pessimists prepare for an exam?
tasks.note: SB 5b (вопрос по статье) → Blank на ключевые слова по напечатанной статье (MODEL); пункты 3–7 — как защитные пессимисты решают каждую проблему из картинки
tasks.context: Why negative thinking can be positive. Everybody thinks that it’s better to be an optimist than a pessimist (even pessimists think it, of course). People always say ‘Cheer up. Don’t worry, be happy. Smile.’ But in fact there’s a kind of pessimism – called ‘defensive pessimism’ – that can lead to very positive results, according to Julie K. Norem, a professor of psychology at Wellesley College, Massachusetts. ‘Defensive pessimism is a strategy used in specific situations to manage anxiety, fear, and worry,’ says Norem. Studies show that 30 to 35 per cent of Americans use it to help them in their lives, and they’re often very successful people. Defensive pessimists think about future situations and prepare for them by imagining all the things that can go wrong. For example, if a defensive pessimist has an important exam, they think this: I’ll go to the wrong place. I’ll feel thirsty or hungry. My pen will run out or my pencil will break. I’ll be tired. I’ll be late. Then they look at each possible problem and plan how to avoid it. So for the exam situation, they go to bed early and have a good night’s sleep; they find out in advance exactly where the exam is; they eat a good breakfast, and take lots of pens and pencils, and a bottle of water; and they leave home early. That puts them in control, and it means that the exam will be better than for an optimist, who just thinks ‘Oh, everything will be fine!’ Because sometimes everything goes wrong, and it’s good to be prepared.

exercises.prompt: The man is a defensive pessimist and he is flying tomorrow. Write how he can avoid each problem.

questions.text: I’ll go to the wrong terminal.
It’ll be too cold on the plane.
The airline food will be terrible.

criteria: gives a sensible solution for each of the five problems
uses can / should / will + infinitive or imperatives correctly
sentences are clear and grammatically correct

exercises.prompt: Write your opinion about defensive pessimism.

questions.text: Do you think defensive pessimism is a good strategy? Why (not)?
Do you ever use it? When?

criteria: gives an opinion with a reason
gives a real example from their life
uses will / won’t for predictions correctly if they write what they imagine

tasks.instruction: Ask and answer the questions. Say why
tasks.note: SB 6 Speaking «Do you think…?» + ответы из рамки (I hope so / I doubt it…) → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: Speaking practice in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You and the student ask each other ‘Do you think…?’ questions and answer with I hope so / I hope not / I think so / I don’t think so / Maybe / Perhaps / I doubt it / Probably (not) / Definitely (not), and then say why. The questions: Do you think you’ll… have a nice weekend? pass your next English exam? get a good (or better) job in the future? make some new friends on your next holiday? live to be 100? get to the end of this book? find the love of your life? Ask the student a question, listen to the answer and the reason, react, and answer their questions too. One question at a time.
exercises.goal: Ask and answer ‘Do you think you’ll…?’ and say why.
exercises.opener: Do you think you’ll have a nice weekend?
criteria: answers with a short response from the box (I hope so, I doubt it, Probably not…) and a reason
asks at least three questions with Do you think you’ll…?
uses will / won’t + infinitive correctly in the reasons

steps.example: I hope so. I think the weather will be good and I’m going to the beach.

steps.text: Ask about an English exam and a job
steps.example: Do you think you’ll pass your next English exam?
Do you think you’ll live to be 100?

steps.text: Ask about the love of your life
steps.example: Do you think you’ll find the love of your life?
